```{r}
set.seed(4242)
sim_data <- function(n = 1000, pi = 0.5) {
  w <- rnorm(n)
  a <- rbinom(n, 1, pi)
  y <- cos(w) + w*a + a + rnorm(n)
  data.frame(y, a, w)
}
d <- sim_data(n = 500)
```

## 1.7. Large sample comparison: unbalanced simple randomization

design with 2:1 randomization $\pi = P(A=1) = 2/3$. Do the results look
different compared to the balanced simple randomization design from the previous

## 1.8 Stratified randomization: ATE

Consider the following data generation process with block randomization

```{r}
sim_data_stratified <- function(n, block_size = 6L) {
  w <- rnorm(n)
  s <- as.integer(w < -0.67) # stratification variable as grouping of baseline
                             # covariate w
  a <- integer(n)

  for (stratum in unique(s)) {
    idx <- which(s == stratum)

    blocks <- split(idx, ceiling(seq_along(idx) / block_size))
    for (block in blocks) {
      allocation <- rep(sample(0:1), length.out = block_size)
      allocation <- sample(allocation)

      a[block] <- allocation[seq_along(block)]
    }
  }

  y <- cos(w) + w * a + a + rnorm(n)
  data.frame(y, a, w, s = as.factor(s))
}

d_stratified <- sim_data_stratified(n = 1e3)
```

Use `targeted::cate` to estimate the ATE with the ANHECOVA estimator, adjusting
for baseline covariate `w` for the following large data sample.

```{r}
d_stratified <- sim_data_stratified(n = 1e5)
```

## 1.9 Stratified randomization: ANHECOVA and ANOVA comparison

Compare the ANHECOVA and ANOVA implementation with `cate` with the following
model-based estimator that adjusts for the stratification variable. Use the
same large data sample from the previous exercise. Describe what you observe.


```{r}
fit_model <- glm(y ~ a + s, data = d_stratified)
```

0] - E[Y(0) | S = 0]$. Use the same working model as the ANHECOVA estimator of
